He continued westward with the pilgrims, and before they knew it, summer had arrived. The warm southern breeze was just beginning to stir, and the plum rains fell in fine threads. p.src: The master and his three disciples endured the scorching heat as they traveled. Suddenly, beside the road, they saw two rows of tall willows. From their shade emerged an old woman leading a small child by her right hand. She called loudly to the Tang Monk, “Monk, go no farther! Turn your horse around quickly and head east, for every road westward leads to death.” Sanzang was so alarmed that he leapt from his horse, saluted her with joined palms, and said, “Venerable bodhisattva, the ancients said, ‘In the boundless sea, fish may leap at will; beneath the vast sky, birds may freely fly.’ How can it be that there is no road westward?” Pointing west, the old woman said, “Five or six li from here lies the Kingdom of Dharma-Destroying. Its king incurred a grudge in a former life and now, in this life, commits sins without cause. Two years ago, he made a great vow before all Heaven to kill ten thousand monks. Over these two years, one after another, he has killed nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-six unknown monks. Now he awaits four monks of renown to make the full ten thousand and fulfill his vow. If you enter that city, you will all be delivering yourselves into the hands of the King of Death.” Hearing this, Sanzang became afraid and said, trembling, “Venerable bodhisattva, I am deeply grateful for your kindness and cannot thank you enough. But may I ask whether there is some convenient road by which we can avoid entering the city? This poor monk will go around it.” The old woman laughed. “There is no way around it, no way around it. Only one who can fly could pass over it.” Bajie, standing nearby, boasted, “Granny, don't speak in riddles. We can all fly.”

p.src: With his fiery eyes and golden pupils, the Pilgrim could truly distinguish good from evil: the old woman and the child she led were none other than the Bodhisattva Guanyin and the Child Sudhana. He hastily prostrated himself and cried, “Bodhisattva, forgive your disciple for failing to welcome you!” The Bodhisattva gently rose upon an auspicious cloud. Elder Tang was so startled that he did not know where to stand and could only remain kneeling and kowtowing; Bajie and Sha Monk also hastily knelt and worshiped toward the sky. In a moment, the auspicious cloud drifted into the distance and returned directly to the Southern Sea.

p.src: The Pilgrim rose, helped his master up, and said, “Please rise. The Bodhisattva has already returned to her sacred mountain.” Sanzang rose and said, “Wukong, since you recognized the Bodhisattva, why did you not tell us sooner?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Before you had even finished asking your question, I bowed down. How was that not soon enough?” Bajie and Sha Monk said to the Pilgrim, “Thanks to the Bodhisattva's warning, we know that the Kingdom of Dharma-Destroying must lie ahead and that they intend to kill monks. What are we to do?” The Pilgrim said, “Fool, do not be afraid. We have faced vicious demons and savage monsters, entered tigers' dens and dragons' pools, and never yet suffered harm. Those here are merely ordinary mortals of a human kingdom. What is there to fear? The trouble is that this is no place to stay. Night is approaching, and villagers or traders returning from the city may see that we are monks and spread the word, which would place us in danger. Let us first lead Master off the main road and find a secluded place where we can discuss our plans.” Sanzang followed his advice, and the whole party slipped off the road and settled down below a hollow. The Pilgrim said, “Brothers, guard Master well, while old Sun changes his form and goes into the city to take a look. I shall find a secluded route by which we can pass through during the night.” Sanzang cautioned him, “Disciple, do not take this lightly. The king's law shows no mercy, so you must be careful.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Do not worry, do not worry. Old Sun knows what to do.”

p.src: There he went, fluttering and flitting through the city's avenues and markets, skirting the eaves and drawing close to the corners of houses. As he flew on, he suddenly saw a curved row of houses around a street corner, with a lantern hanging before every door. He said, “Are these people celebrating the Lantern Festival? Why have they all lit lanterns in a row?” He stiffened his wings and flew closer to examine them. On a square lantern before the house in the middle were written the six characters, “Lodging for Traveling Merchants,” and beneath them another four, “Wang Xiaoer's Inn.” Only then did the Pilgrim realize that it was an inn. He craned his head to look inside and saw eight or nine men who had all finished supper, loosened their clothes, removed their headcloths, washed their hands and feet, and gone to bed. The Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “Master will be able to get through.” But how did he know that they could get through? A mischievous scheme had entered his mind: once those men were asleep, he intended to steal their clothes and headcloths so that the pilgrims could disguise themselves as laymen and enter the city.

p.src: Alas! But matters would not go as he wished. While he was still considering his plan, the innkeeper came forward and warned them, “Gentlemen, take care. Good men and rogues alike come through this place, so each of you must watch your clothing and luggage carefully.” Now, what traveling merchant would not be cautious? After hearing the innkeeper's warning, they became more vigilant still. They all climbed out of bed and said, “What our host says is right. We travelers are weary, and we fear that once asleep we may not wake quickly; if something should be lost in the meantime, what could we do? Take our clothes, headcloths, and travel pouches inside for safekeeping, and return them to us at daybreak when we rise to leave.” Wang Xiaoer accordingly carried every last article of clothing into his own room. Impatient by nature, the Pilgrim spread his wings, flew inside, and alighted on a headcloth rack. He then watched Wang Xiaoer go to the entrance, take down the lantern, lower the hanging screen, and close the doors and windows before returning to his room, undressing, and lying down to sleep. Wang Xiaoer had a wife and two children, and the children kept wailing and making such a racket that they would not settle down to sleep. His wife, meanwhile, took up a tattered garment and continued patching and mending it, showing no sign of going to sleep either.

p.src: Pilgrim thought to himself, “If I wait until this old woman falls asleep before acting, won’t that delay Master?” Fearing, too, that the night would deepen and the city gates would close, he could restrain himself no longer. He flew down and pounced upon the lamp. Truly: He risked himself by plunging into flame, scorching his brow to seek a remnant of life. The lamp immediately went out. He shook himself and changed again, this time into a rat. After squeaking twice, he jumped down, seized the clothes and headcloths, and made for the door. The old woman cried in alarm, “Old man, this is terrible! A night rat has turned into a spirit!” Hearing this, Pilgrim played another trick. Blocking the door, he shouted sternly, “Wang Xiao’er, do not listen to your wife’s nonsense. I am no night rat turned spirit. An honest man does nothing under cover of darkness. I am none other than the Great Sage Equaling Heaven descended to the mortal world, protecting the Tang Monk on his journey to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Your king is without the Way, so I have come especially to borrow these clothes and headgear to disguise my master. Once we have passed through the city, I shall return them at once.” When Wang Xiao’er heard this, he scrambled out of bed. Groping in the pitch-black room and flustered as he was, he grabbed his trousers for a shirt; he could get neither the left side on nor the right.

p.src: The Great Sage used a drawing spell and was soon riding a cloud out of the city. He then wheeled around and went straight to the edge of the hollow beside the road. Seeing the bright stars and clear moon, Tripitaka leaned out and peered intently. When he saw Pilgrim approaching, he called, “Disciple, can we get through the Kingdom of Dharma-Destroyers?” Pilgrim came forward, set down the clothes, and said, “Master, if we are to pass through the Kingdom of Dharma-Destroyers, we cannot remain monks.” Pigsy said, “Brother, whom are you trying to coerce? It is easy enough to stop being monks. We need only go six months without shaving our heads, and the hair will grow back.” Pilgrim said, “How can we wait six months? We must all become laymen this very moment.” The fool became alarmed and said, “You never think things through when you speak. We are all monks now. If we must become laymen this instant, how are we supposed to wear headcloths? Even if we cinch them around the edges, there is nowhere for the top cords to catch.” Tripitaka rebuked him, “Stop clowning around and attend to the serious business. What exactly is the situation?” Pilgrim said, “Master, I have inspected the city. Though its king is without the Way and kills monks, he is nevertheless a true Son of Heaven, for auspicious light and joyous vapors hover above the walls. I also know the streets within the city. I understand the local speech here as well, and can speak it. I have just borrowed these clothes and headcloths from an inn. Let us disguise ourselves as laymen, enter the city, and obtain lodging. At the fourth watch we shall rise and have the innkeeper prepare a vegetarian meal. We shall linger until the fifth watch, then keep close to the city gate, leave, and take the main road westward. Even if someone runs into us and detains us, we shall have a plausible defense: we need only say we are imperial envoys from the superior kingdom and that the King of Dharma-Destroyers dared not obstruct us but let us pass.” Friar Sand said, “Elder Brother’s plan is most appropriate. Let us follow it.”

p.src: The elder truly had no choice. He removed his short monastic robe and monk’s cap, put on layman’s clothes, and wrapped a headcloth around his head. Friar Sand changed as well. Pigsy’s head was too large for a headcloth, so Pilgrim took needle and thread, ripped open two headcloths, and sewed them into one, which he draped over Pigsy’s head; then he selected a roomy garment and had him put it on. Afterward, Pilgrim changed into an outfit himself and said, “Gentlemen, when we set out, put away the words ‘master’ and ‘disciple’ for the time being.” Pigsy asked, “If we do away with those words, what shall we call one another?” Pilgrim said, “We must address one another as brothers. Master will be called Master Tang, you will be Master Zhu the Third, Friar Sand will be Master Sha the Fourth, and I shall be Master Sun the Second. Once we reach the inn, you must say nothing and let me alone speak and answer. Whatever trade they ask us about, say only that we are horse dealers, with this white horse as a sample. Say that we are ten brothers and that the four of us have come ahead to rent rooms and sell horses. The innkeeper will surely treat us hospitably. After we have enjoyed his hospitality and are about to leave, I shall pick up a shard of roof tile, transform it into a piece of silver to thank him, and then we shall be on our way.” The elder had no choice but to comply.

p.src: The four hurriedly led the horse, shouldered the luggage, and ran over to the city. This was a peaceful realm, and though the night watch had begun, the gates had not yet been closed, so they went straight in. When they reached the entrance of Wang Xiao’er’s inn, they heard people shouting inside. One said, “My headcloth is gone.” Another said, “My clothes are gone.” Pilgrim merely pretended to know nothing and led the others to lodge at an establishment diagonally opposite. That establishment had not yet taken in its lantern, so he approached the door and called, “Innkeeper, do you have a vacant room where we may spend the night?” A woman inside answered, “Yes, yes, we do. Please go upstairs, gentlemen.” Before she had finished speaking, a man came to take the horse, and Pilgrim handed it over to be led inside. He led his master past the shadow of the lantern and straight through the upstairs doorway, where there were convenient tables and chairs. They pushed open the lattice window and all sat down in the moonlight. Presently someone came to light a lamp, but Pilgrim blocked the doorway and blew it out in one breath, saying, “With such a bright moon, we need no lamp.”

p.src: No sooner had she gone downstairs than another maid brought four bowls of clear tea, which Pilgrim took from her. Then a woman of about fifty-seven or fifty-eight came up from below, climbed straight to the upper floor, and stood beside them. She asked, “Where have you gentlemen come from? What valuable goods are you carrying?” Pilgrim said, “We come from the north and have several horses of no great quality to sell.” The woman said, “You horse dealers are still quite young.” Pilgrim said, “This is Master Tang, this is Third Master Zhu, and this is Fourth Master Sha. Your humble servant is Second Master Sun.” The woman laughed. “All different surnames, I see.” Pilgrim said, “Indeed, we bear different surnames but live as one family. There are ten brothers among us; we four came ahead to rent rooms and prepare a meal, while the other six are resting outside the city with a herd of horses, since it was too late to enter. Once we have rented rooms, they will all come in tomorrow morning. We shall not return home until the horses are sold.” The woman asked, “How many horses are in the herd?” Pilgrim replied, “A hundred and ten or so, large and small. They are all about the size of this horse of mine, though their coats differ.” The woman laughed. “Second Master Sun truly knows how a traveler should conduct his business. Fortunately you came to my establishment; no other household would dare lodge you. My grounds are spacious, with all the necessary troughs and stalls as well as fodder. Even several hundred horses could be kept here. There is just one thing: my establishment has kept this inn for many years and has acquired a humble name. My late husband’s surname was Zhao, but unhappily he passed away long ago. My inn is called the Widow Zhao Inn. My inn offers guests three grades of service. Let us speak plainly before behaving as friends: first we should settle the room charge, so that the account will be easy afterward.” Pilgrim said, “That is reasonable. What are these three grades of service your establishment provides? As the saying goes, ‘Goods have high, middle, and low prices, but guests from near and far should be treated alike.’ Why do you speak of three kinds of treatment? Tell me about them, if you please.” Widow Zhao said, “Here we have upper, middle, and lower grades. The upper grade provides a banquet of five fruits and five vegetable dishes, with a table spread with lion-and-immortal molded sweets for every two guests. Young women are invited to sing and spend the night with you. The charge is five mace of silver per person, room included.” Pilgrim laughed. “That is cheap! Where I come from, five mace of silver would not even be enough to hire a young woman.” The widow continued, “For the middle grade, there is a shared platter with only fruit and warmed wine. You may pour it yourselves and play drinking games, without young women. The charge is only two mace of silver per person.” Pilgrim said, “Cheaper still. And what is the lower grade like?” The woman replied, “I would not dare describe it before honored guests.” Pilgrim said, “There is no harm in telling us. Then we can choose the most economical.” The woman said, “In the lower grade, no one waits upon you. There is plain ready-made rice in the pot, and guests may eat as much as they please. When they are full, they take some straw, spread a bed on the floor, and sleep wherever convenient. At daybreak they may give whatever few coppers they wish for the meal; we never haggle over it.” When Eight Rules heard this, he cried, “What luck! What luck! Old Zhu has found just the bargain for him! Let me eat my fill straight from the pot, then sleep by the stove, damn it!” Pilgrim said, “Brother, what are you talking about? As men of the road, where could we not earn a few taels of silver? Bring us the upper-grade service.”

Pilgrim replied, “A hundred and ten or so, large and small. They are all about the size of this horse of mine, though their coats differ.”
The woman laughed. “Second Master Sun truly knows how a traveler should conduct his business.
Fortunately you came to my establishment; no other household would dare lodge you.
My grounds are spacious, with all the necessary troughs and stalls as well as fodder. Even several hundred horses could be kept here.
There is just one thing: my establishment has kept this inn for many years and has acquired a humble name.
My late husband’s surname was Zhao, but unhappily he passed away long ago.
My inn is called the Widow Zhao Inn.
My inn offers guests three grades of service.
Let us speak plainly before behaving as friends: first we should settle the room charge, so that the account will be easy afterward.”
Pilgrim said, “That is reasonable.
What are these three grades of service your establishment provides?
As the saying goes, ‘Goods have high, middle, and low prices, but guests from near and far should be treated alike.’
Why do you speak of three kinds of treatment?
Tell me about them, if you please.”
Widow Zhao said, “Here we have upper, middle, and lower grades.

The upper grade provides a banquet of five fruits and five vegetable dishes, with a table spread with lion-and-immortal molded sweets for every two guests. Young women are invited to sing and spend the night with you. The charge is five mace of silver per person, room included.”
Pilgrim laughed. “That is cheap! Where I come from, five mace of silver would not even be enough to hire a young woman.”

The widow continued, “For the middle grade, there is a shared platter with only fruit and warmed wine. You may pour it yourselves and play drinking games, without young women. The charge is only two mace of silver per person.”
Pilgrim said, “Cheaper still.
And what is the lower grade like?”
The woman replied, “I would not dare describe it before honored guests.”
Pilgrim said, “There is no harm in telling us. Then we can choose the most economical.”
The woman said, “In the lower grade, no one waits upon you. There is plain ready-made rice in the pot, and guests may eat as much as they please.
When they are full, they take some straw, spread a bed on the floor, and sleep wherever convenient.
At daybreak they may give whatever few coppers they wish for the meal; we never haggle over it.”
When Eight Rules heard this, he cried, “What luck! What luck!
Old Zhu has found just the bargain for him!
Let me eat my fill straight from the pot, then sleep by the stove, damn it!”
Pilgrim said, “Brother, what are you talking about?
As men of the road, where could we not earn a few taels of silver?
Bring us the upper-grade service.”

p.src: The woman was delighted and immediately called out, “Bring the finest tea, and have the kitchen hurry with the food.” She went downstairs and busily ordered, “Slaughter chickens and geese, and cook cured meat to go with the rice.” Then she called, “Kill a pig and a sheep too. If we cannot use them all today, they will keep for tomorrow. See that the wine is good, cook white rice, and roll white flour into flatcakes.” Hearing this upstairs, Tripitaka said, “Second Master Sun, what are we to do? She is slaughtering chickens and geese and killing pigs and sheep. If she serves them to us, who among us, lifelong vegetarians, would dare eat them?” Pilgrim said, “I have a plan.” He went to the head of the stairs, stamped his foot, and called, “Mother Zhao, come upstairs.” The woman came up and asked, “What are your orders, Second Master?” Pilgrim said, “Do not take life today. We are observing a fast.” The widow asked in surprise, “Do you gentlemen abstain from meat always, or only on certain days of the month?” Pilgrim replied, “Neither. Ours is called the Gengshen fast. Today is a Gengshen day, so we must fast. Once the third watch has passed, it will be Xinyou, and we may break the fast. Leave the slaughtering until tomorrow. For now, prepare some vegetarian dishes, and we will still pay the full upper-grade price.”

p.src: The woman was more delighted than ever. She ran downstairs and ordered, “Do not slaughter them! Do not slaughter them! Fetch some wood ears, Fujian bamboo shoots, tofu, and wheat gluten. Pull some greens from the garden, make vermicelli soup, leaven dough and steam rolls, then cook white rice and brew fragrant tea.” Well now! The cooks were all practiced hands who prepared such fare every day. In no time everything was ready and laid out upstairs, together with the lion-and-immortal molded sweets already on hand, and the four travelers ate as freely as they pleased. The widow also asked, “Do you drink meatless wine?” Pilgrim replied, “Only Master Tang abstains. The rest of us will have a few cups.” The widow brought another pot of warmed wine. Just as the three of them had poured their first cups, they suddenly heard a clattering crash of boards. Pilgrim asked, “Mother, what household object has fallen over downstairs?” The widow said, “Nothing has fallen. Several tenants from my little estate came late to deliver their rent rice, so I told them to sleep downstairs. Since you gentlemen arrived and I had no one else to send, I told them to carry a sedan chair to the pleasure quarter and invite a young woman to entertain you. The chair poles must have struck the floorboards.” Pilgrim said, “You should have told me sooner! Quickly, do not send for them. For one thing, this is our day of fasting; for another, our brothers have not yet arrived. Let us wait until they all enter tomorrow, then hire one courtesan for each man and amuse ourselves here until the horses are sold and we depart.” The widow said, “A fine idea, a fine idea! It will preserve good feeling and conserve your strength.” She ordered, “Carry the sedan chair back inside; do not go to invite them.” The four travelers finished their wine and food; the utensils were cleared away, and everyone dispersed.

p.src: Tripitaka whispered in Pilgrim’s ear, “Where are we to sleep?” Pilgrim replied, “We will sleep right here upstairs.” Tripitaka said, “That will not be safe. We are all exhausted. If we fall asleep and someone in this household comes to tidy up, one of our caps may slip off and reveal a shaven head. If they realize we are monks and raise an outcry, what shall we do?” Pilgrim said, “You are right!” He went to the front of the upper floor and stamped his foot again. The widow came back upstairs and asked, “What further orders have you, Master Sun?” Pilgrim asked, “Where are we to sleep?” The woman replied, “Upstairs is an excellent place to sleep. There are no mosquitoes, a southerly breeze is blowing, and with the windows wide open it is wonderfully comfortable.” Pilgrim said, “We cannot sleep here. Our Third Master Zhu suffers somewhat from cold and damp, Fourth Master Sha has a draft-sensitive shoulder, Elder Brother Tang can sleep only in darkness, and I too am a little troubled by bright light. This is no place for us to sleep.”

p.src: The old woman went downstairs and leaned against the counter, sighing. Her daughter, carrying a child in her arms, came up and said, “Mother, as the saying goes, ‘Sit ten days at the head of the rapids, and in one day you can pass nine.’ It is summer now, so although there is little business, once autumn comes there will be more trade than we can handle. Why are you sighing?” The woman said, “My child, I am not fretting over the lack of business. This evening, just as I was about to close the inn around the first watch, these four horse dealers came to rent rooms and asked for the finest hospitality. I had truly hoped to earn a few pieces of silver from them, but they eat only vegetarian food, so there is no money to be made. That is why I sighed.” Her daughter said, “Since they have eaten here, they will hardly go to another inn. Tomorrow we can prepare meat and wine for them, so why should we not make money?” The woman continued, “They all claim to be ill, afraid of drafts, and averse to light, and each wants to sleep somewhere dark. But think: all the rooms in our house have only single-layer tiles. Where could we find a dark place? We may as well give them this one meal and tell them to seek lodging elsewhere.” Her daughter said, “Mother, our house does have a dark place, with no draft at all. It would be excellent, truly excellent.” The woman asked, “Where is that?” Her daughter replied, “When Father was alive, he made a large chest. It is four feet wide, seven feet long, and about three feet high; six or seven people could sleep inside it. Let them sleep in the chest.” The woman said, “I wonder whether that would do. Let me ask them. Master Sun, our humble dwelling has no other dark place, only a large chest that admits neither wind nor light. How would you like to sleep inside it?” The Pilgrim said, “Good, good, good!” She immediately had several attendants carry out the chest and open its lid, then invited them to come downstairs.

p.src: The Pilgrim led his master while Friar Sand carried the luggage, and by the lamplight they went straight to the chest. Ignoring whether it was proper or not, Pigsy clambered into the chest first. Friar Sand passed in the luggage, helped Tripitaka inside, and then climbed in himself. The Pilgrim asked, “Where is my horse?” An attendant nearby replied, “The horse is tethered in the rear building, eating its fodder.” The Pilgrim said, “Bring it here, carry over its manger, and tether it snugly beside the chest.” Only then did he climb inside and call, “Madam Zhao, put down the lid, insert the locking pin, and fasten the lock. And please look for any place where light gets through and paste some paper over it. Come early tomorrow morning to open it.” The widow said, “You are exceedingly cautious.” Thereafter everyone shut their doors and went to sleep, and nothing more need be said of them.

p.src: Now the four of them were inside the chest—and what misery it was! For one thing, they were unaccustomed to wearing headcloths; for another, the weather was hot, and the enclosed air was stifling, with scarcely a breath of wind entering. They all removed their headcloths and took off their clothes. Having brought no fans, they could only flap their monks’ caps to cool themselves. Each pressed against the next until, around the second watch, they finally fell asleep. Only the Pilgrim, intent on stirring up trouble, could not sleep. He reached out and gave Pigsy’s leg a pinch. The fool drew up his leg and grunted, “Go to sleep! After all our hardship, how can you still have the heart to pinch and paw at people for sport?” Playing his trick, the Pilgrim said, “Our original capital was five thousand taels. The horses we sold earlier brought three thousand, and now the two saddlebags contain four thousand in ready silver. If this herd also sells for three thousand, we shall have doubled our capital. That is enough, more than enough.” Pigsy was bent on sleeping and gave him no answer.

p.src: Little did they know that the inn’s waiters, water carriers, and fire tenders had long been in league with bandits. Hearing the Pilgrim speak of so much silver, some of them slipped out and gathered more than twenty thieves, who came with torches and weapons to rob the horse dealers and burst through the gate. Widow Zhao and the women of her family were so terrified that they shut themselves in their rooms, leaving the bandits to do as they pleased outside. The thieves had no interest in the inn’s household goods; they sought only the guests. Finding no trace of them upstairs, they lit torches and searched all around. In the courtyard they saw a large chest, with a white horse tethered to one of its feet. Its lid was tightly locked, and they could not overturn it. The thieves said, “Travelers are always full of tricks. Judging by how heavy this chest is, their baggage and valuables must be locked inside. Why not steal the horse, carry the chest out of the city, then break it open and divide the contents among ourselves?” The thieves found ropes and carrying poles, hoisted the chest, and set off with it swaying to and fro. Pigsy woke and said, “Brother, go to sleep. Why are you rocking the chest?” The Pilgrim said, “Keep quiet. No one is rocking it.” Tripitaka and Friar Sand suddenly woke as well and asked, “Who is carrying us?” The Pilgrim said, “Do not shout, do not shout. Let them carry us. If they carry us all the way to the Western Heaven, it will save us the trouble of walking.”

p.src: Having succeeded, the thieves did not head west but carried the chest eastward instead. They killed the soldiers guarding the gate, opened the city gate, and escaped. This immediately roused the fire-watchmen and laborers of every shop throughout the city’s streets and markets, and they all reported the crime to the commander of the city patrol and the Eastern Ward Military Office. As the matter fell within their own responsibility, the commander and the military commissioner immediately mustered mounted troops and archers and left the city in pursuit of the thieves. Seeing the strength of the government troops, the thieves dared not resist. They abandoned the great chest and the white horse and fled separately into the wilderness. The government troops failed to catch even half a bandit, but they recovered the chest and seized the horse, then returned in triumph. He led the troops back into the city, had the chest carried to his headquarters, and, together with the military commissioner, wrote out a seal and sealed it shut. He ordered men to guard it until dawn, when they would report to the throne and request a ruling. The government troops then dispersed, and nothing more need be said of them.

p.src: Meanwhile, inside the chest, Elder Tang reproached the Pilgrim, saying, “You wretched monkey, you have brought about my death! Had we been outside when they caught us and delivered us to the king of the Dharma-Destroying Kingdom, we might still have argued our case. But now we have been locked in a chest, carried off by thieves, and then seized by government troops. When we face the king tomorrow, we shall be ready at hand for him to put to the sword. Will that not complete his tally of ten thousand?” The Pilgrim said, “If someone outside opens the chest and drags us out, we shall either be bound or hanged. Bear with it a little longer, and we shall avoid both ropes and hanging. When we meet that foolish king tomorrow, old Sun will know how to answer him. I guarantee that not a hair on your body will be harmed. Set your mind at ease and get some sleep.”

p.src: When the third watch finally came, Monkey used his magic, drew out his staff, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly became a three-pointed drill. He bored two or three times beside a foot of the cabinet and made a hole. Putting away the drill, he shook himself, changed into a mole cricket, and scrambled out. He resumed his true form, mounted a cloud, and went straight to the gates of the imperial palace. The king was then deep asleep. Monkey performed the divine art of universal assembly through manifold bodies, plucked every hair from his left arm, breathed an immortal breath upon them, and cried, “Change!” They all changed into little Monkeys. He also plucked every hair from his right arm, breathed an immortal breath upon them, and cried, “Change!” They all changed into sleep-inducing insects. He recited the true-word spell “Om” and ordered the local earth god to lead the host in scattering throughout the inner palace, the Five Commissions and Six Ministries, and every government office and official residence. Every person of rank was to be given a sleep-inducing insect, so that all would sleep soundly and none could turn over. Then he took the Gold-Banded Staff in hand, weighed and brandished it, and cried, “Precious one, change!” It instantly became hundreds upon hundreds of razors. He took one and told each little Monkey to take one too; then they all went to shave heads throughout the inner palace, the Five Commissions, the Six Ministries, and every government office. Ah! Indeed:

p.src: Now in the inner palace, before dawn the palace maids and ladies-in-waiting rose to wash and dress, only to find that every one of them had lost her hair; the eunuchs of every rank who served within the palace had also lost all their hair. They all surged together to the outside of the royal bedchamber and played music to wake the sleepers, each with tears in their eyes but none daring to say what had happened. Before long, the three palace queens awoke, and they too had lost all their hair. They hurriedly brought a lamp to look beneath the imperial bed and saw a monk asleep inside the brocade covers. One queen could not help crying out, and her voice startled the king awake. The king opened his eyes in alarm and saw the queen’s bare head. Scrambling up, he said, “My dear consort, how did you come to be like this?” The queen replied, “Your Majesty is the same.” The emperor felt his head and was so terrified that his three corpses groaned and his seven souls flew from him. “What am I to do?” he cried. As he panicked, the consorts of the six courts, the palace maids and ladies-in-waiting, and all the eunuchs appeared. Every one of them knelt with a bare head and said, “Your Majesty, we have all become monks!” At the sight, tears ran from the king’s eyes. “This must be because I have slaughtered monks…” he said. Then he issued an order: “None of you is to speak of our losing our hair, lest the civil and military ministers condemn the realm for its unrighteousness. For now, let us all go to the throne hall and hold court.”

u.src: Now in the inner palace, before dawn the palace maids and ladies-in-waiting rose to wash and dress, only to find that every one of them had lost her hair;
the eunuchs of every rank who served within the palace had also lost all their hair.
They all surged together to the outside of the royal bedchamber and played music to wake the sleepers, each with tears in their eyes but none daring to say what had happened.
Before long, the three palace queens awoke, and they too had lost all their hair.
They hurriedly brought a lamp to look beneath the imperial bed and saw a monk asleep inside the brocade covers. One queen could not help crying out, and her voice startled the king awake.
The king opened his eyes in alarm and saw the queen’s bare head. Scrambling up, he said, “My dear consort, how did you come to be like this?”
The queen replied, “Your Majesty is the same.”
The emperor felt his head and was so terrified that his three corpses groaned and his seven souls flew from him. “What am I to do?” he cried.

As he panicked, the consorts of the six courts, the palace maids and ladies-in-waiting, and all the eunuchs appeared. Every one of them knelt with a bare head and said, “Your Majesty, we have all become monks!”

At the sight, tears ran from the king’s eyes. “This must be because I have slaughtered monks…” he said. Then he issued an order: “None of you is to speak of our losing our hair, lest the civil and military ministers condemn the realm for its unrighteousness.
For now, let us all go to the throne hall and hold court.”
